articles.title: Signs Your Roof May Need Repair
articles.metaTitle: 8 Signs Your Roof May Need Repair | Timber Roofing
articles.description: The visible and not-so-visible signs a North Texas roof needs attention, and which ones mean call today rather than next month.
articles.excerpt: Most roofs give warning before they fail. The trouble is that the warnings are easy to miss from ground level.

body.text: Roofs rarely fail all at once. They give notice, usually for a year or two, and the notice is easy to overlook because most of it happens above eye level. Here is what to look for, roughly in order of how urgently it should be dealt with.
Interior signs you should act on quickly
A stain on a ceiling or an upstairs wall means water has already been inside for a while. Drywall does not stain on the first drip. If the stain grows or darkens after rain, the intrusion is active.

Damp or matted attic insulation is the same signal, caught earlier. So is a musty smell upstairs that you cannot place. In a hot Texas attic, chronic moisture becomes a mold problem faster than most homeowners expect.
Water travels. A stain on your ceiling is almost never directly under the entry point, which is why patching where the stain is fixes nothing.
Exterior signs visible from the ground

items: Granules collecting where downspouts discharge, or a heavy deposit after a storm
Shingles that look darker or lighter in irregular patches across a slope
Visible curling, cupping, or lifted edges along the courses
Missing shingles, or shingle pieces in the yard and beds
Dented gutters, downspouts, or roof vents, which point at hail
Rust streaks or lifted metal at a chimney or wall line

body.text: The signs you cannot see

This is the frustrating part. Hail bruising and broken wind seals — the two most common forms of storm damage in North Texas — are effectively invisible from a driveway. A shingle that was folded back by wind and settled again looks completely normal from below and is no longer bonded to anything.

Cracked pipe boots are the same story. The rubber collar around a plumbing vent splits after eight or ten Texas summers, and there is no way to see it without getting eyes on the roof. It is one of the cheapest repairs on a roof and one of the most common leak sources.
When to call rather than watch
Call promptly if you have an active leak, visible daylight in the attic, missing shingles, or a stain that changed after the last rain. Those are not wait-and-see items.

For everything else, an inspection is the sensible next step and it costs nothing. The point is to find out whether you are looking at a small repair or the beginning of a bigger conversation, and to find out now rather than after the drywall is involved.

articles.title: Repair or Replace: How to Evaluate a Roof
articles.metaTitle: Roof Repair or Replacement? | Timber Roofing
articles.description: A practical framework for deciding between roof repair and full replacement, including the questions worth asking any contractor.
articles.excerpt: There is a real answer to this question, and it is not always the more expensive one.

body.text: Plenty of roofs get replaced that only needed a repair, and plenty get repaired repeatedly when they should have been replaced two years ago. Both are expensive mistakes. Here is how to think about it.
The four factors that actually decide it

items: How widespread the damage is. Damage confined to one slope or a few details is a repair. Damage scattered across every elevation is not.
How much life the roof has left. Fixing a detail on a roof with twelve good years ahead of it is money well spent. Doing the same work on a roof with two years left is not.
Whether the material can be matched. Sometimes a repair is technically sound but the color match is poor enough that appearance becomes the deciding factor.
What is underneath. If tear-off is going to reveal soft decking or old water damage, that changes the arithmetic entirely.

body.text: Cases where repair is usually right

A single failed pipe boot. Wind damage confined to one windward slope. A flashing detail at a chimney that was sealed instead of built correctly. A valley that has worn through while the rest of the field is sound. In each case the roof is fundamentally healthy and one component has failed.
Cases where replacement is usually right

Hail bruising across multiple slopes. Repeated leaks in different locations over consecutive seasons. Bare shingle mat where the granules are gone entirely. A visible sag in the roof plane. Any situation where you have already paid for two or three repairs in three years.
Three leaks in three seasons in three different places is a roof telling you it is finished. One leak is an event.
Questions worth asking whoever inspected it

items: Can you show me a photograph of the actual failure point?
How many years do you think the rest of the roof has left, and why?
If we repair this, what is the most likely next thing to fail?
What would you do if it were your house?

body.text: The answers tell you a great deal. Someone who can show you the specific failure and reason through the remaining life of the roof is thinking about your roof. Someone who moves straight to replacement without either is thinking about something else.

If storm damage is involved and you have a policy, get the damage documented before you make a decision either way. Documentation close in time to the event is more useful than documentation months later.

articles.title: What Hail Damage Can Look Like
articles.metaTitle: What Hail Damage Looks Like | Timber Roofing
articles.description: How hail damage actually appears on asphalt shingles, gutters, and vents — and why it so often does not look like damage at all.
articles.excerpt: People expect holes. Hail damage on an asphalt roof looks more like a bruise.

body.text: North Texas sits in one of the most hail-active regions in the country, and hail damage is the single most common reason a roof here gets replaced ahead of schedule. It is also the most commonly missed, because it does not look the way people expect.
On asphalt shingles

A hail impact knocks granules loose and fractures the mat underneath. What you see is a dark, roughly circular spot where the granules are gone — often slightly soft if you press it. The shingle is still sitting there doing its job, more or less, but the asphalt underneath is now exposed to UV and the clock has been accelerated.
Two things distinguish hail from ordinary wear. The pattern is random and scattered rather than following the courses, and it is directional — heavier on the slopes facing the storm's approach.
On soft metals
This is where hail is easiest to confirm, and it is why any decent inspection starts by looking at things other than the roof.

items: Gutters and downspouts: dimples and dents along the exposed faces
Roof vents and turbine housings: dents on the top surfaces
AC condenser fins: flattened or bent
Window screens and mailboxes: dents and tears
Fence caps and metal patio furniture: the same dimpling

body.text: If your gutters and vents are dented, something hit them hard enough to be worth checking on the roof above them.
Where it shows up first
Ridge and hip caps take impact before field shingles do — they are more exposed and they sit over a bend, which makes them easier to fracture. Any careful inspection looks there early.
Why it matters even without a leak

This is the part that costs homeowners the most. Hail damage frequently does not leak for a year or more. The roof looks fine, nothing drips, and by the time it does start leaking, the connection to that specific storm is much harder to establish and any policy window has usually closed.

Which is the argument for getting it documented after the storm rather than after the ceiling stains. The inspection is free, and if there is nothing there, you have a dated record showing the roof was in good condition.
We can document visible damage and describe the roofing scope. We are not a public adjuster or an insurer and cannot tell you what your carrier will decide — be cautious of anyone who says they can.

articles.title: What to Do After a North Texas Storm
articles.metaTitle: What to Do After a Texas Storm | Timber Roofing
articles.description: A practical order of operations after hail or high wind hits your home, from immediate safety through documentation and inspection.
articles.excerpt: The first hour matters, and so does not signing anything in it.

body.text: 1. Safety first, and stay off the roof

Do not climb up to look. Wet shingles, loose material, and possible structural damage make that genuinely dangerous, and there is nothing you can see up there that a proper inspection will not find. Watch for downed lines, and stay clear of any ceiling that is bulging or sagging.
2. Contain active water inside

Move furniture and belongings out of the water's path, put down containers, and pull back rugs. If water is pooling above a ceiling, a professional can relieve it safely — do not stand under it and poke at it yourself.
3. Photograph everything, from the ground

items: Interior damage: ceilings, walls, flooring, and belongings
Debris in the yard — shingle pieces, limbs, anything blown loose
Dented gutters, downspouts, vents, screens, and AC fins
Fence damage and downed sections
Wide shots showing the whole house, and close-ups of specific damage

body.text: Photos taken the same day are worth more than photos taken next week. Your phone stamps them with a date, which is exactly the point.
4. Get temporary protection if the roof is open

If there is a visible hole, missing decking, or a large area stripped bare, the priority is keeping water out until a permanent repair can happen. That is a job for someone with the equipment to do it safely.
5. Schedule an inspection — and slow down on the contracts
After a significant hail event, contractors arrive in numbers, some from several states away. Most are legitimate. Some are not, and the ones who are not rely on you feeling rushed.
Ask anyone at your door where they are based, how long they have worked in this area, and whether they will be reachable in two years. It is a fair question and a very effective filter.

items: Do not sign anything on the doorstep, including anything described as 'just authorizing an inspection'
Be wary of any offer to cover or waive your deductible
Be wary of anyone who promises a specific insurance outcome
Get the scope in writing, itemized, before you agree to anything

body.text: 6. Contact your insurance carrier yourself

Your claim is your relationship with your insurer. A roofing contractor can document visible damage and describe the roofing scope in specific terms for you to share — that is legitimate and useful. Negotiating your claim on your behalf is not something a roofer is licensed to do.

articles.title: How Often Should a Roof Be Inspected?
articles.metaTitle: How Often Should You Inspect a Roof? | Timber Roofing
articles.description: A sensible inspection schedule for North Texas homes, and the specific events that should prompt an inspection regardless of timing.
articles.excerpt: Once a year is a reasonable baseline. Storms reset the clock.

body.text: The short answer for a North Texas home: once a year, plus after any significant hail or wind event. The longer answer depends on the roof's age and what is growing over it.
The annual baseline

An annual look catches the small failures while they are still small — a cracked pipe boot, debris packed into a valley, a lifted piece of flashing. None of those are expensive to fix. All of them are expensive to ignore for three years.
Events that should prompt an inspection regardless

items: Any hail in your immediate area, even moderate hail
High wind or a severe thunderstorm warning that produced debris
Limbs down in the yard
Any new interior stain, however small
Before buying a home, and before listing one
When you move into a house and do not know the roof's age

body.text: Adjust for your particular situation

Roofs past fifteen years are worth checking more often — the components age faster than the field does, and small failures compound quicker on an older system. Homes under heavy tree canopy also warrant more frequent attention, because the debris load into the valleys never stops.
Newer roofs are not exempt. Installation problems tend to surface in the first few years, and hail does not care how recently the shingles went on.
A documented inspection that finds nothing is still worth having. You now have a dated record of your roof's condition, which is a genuinely useful thing to own.
What a real inspection covers

Field condition on every slope, ridge and hip caps, valleys, rakes and eaves, flashing at every wall and chimney, every penetration and boot, gutter and drainage condition, and the attic where it is accessible. Plus photographs, so you can see it yourself rather than take somebody's word for it.

articles.title: Common Causes of Roof Leaks
articles.metaTitle: Common Causes of Roof Leaks | Timber Roofing
articles.description: Where North Texas roofs actually leak — penetrations, flashing, valleys, and drainage — and why the middle of the roof is rarely the culprit.
articles.excerpt: Roofs mostly do not leak in the middle. They leak where the roof meets something else.

body.text: If you had to guess where a roof leaks, the field — the big open expanse of shingles — would be the obvious answer and almost always the wrong one. Leaks happen at transitions and interruptions. Here is the actual list, roughly in order of frequency on North Texas homes.
1. Pipe boots

The rubber collar sealing around a plumbing vent stack. Texas sun cracks it after eight to twelve years, well before the shingles are finished. It is the most common leak source we find and one of the least expensive to fix.
2. Flashing at walls and chimneys

Wherever the roof meets a vertical surface, metal flashing manages the water. When that flashing is corroded, displaced, or — very commonly — was 'repaired' with a bead of caulk during a previous job, water gets behind it. Sealant shrinks and cracks in this climate, usually within a couple of seasons.
3. Valleys

Valleys carry water from two roof planes at once, which means they handle more volume than anything else on the roof. They wear faster, and they clog with leaves and needles, which backs water up under the shingle edges.
4. Shingles that lost their seal
After a wind event, shingles can be unsealed without being missing. Wind-driven rain then gets underneath them. This is why a roof can start leaking weeks after a storm with nothing visibly wrong.
5. Skylights
A skylight is a hole in the roof with glass in it. The unit itself, the flashing kit around it, and the seal between them are three separate things that can fail.
6. Drainage problems
Clogged or undersized gutters overflow, and the water runs back onto the fascia and up under the roof edge. Missing drip edge makes it worse by giving the water a direct path behind the gutter.
None of the six above requires a new roof. All six are repairs on an otherwise sound roof — which is why a proper diagnosis matters before anyone quotes a replacement.
And the ones that are not the roof at all

HVAC condensate lines, plumbing in a wall, and window flashing all produce stains that get blamed on the roof. A good inspection rules those in or out rather than assuming. If that is what is happening at your house, you should be told so, not sold a roof.

articles.title: How to Document Storm Damage
articles.metaTitle: How to Document Storm Damage | Timber Roofing
articles.description: A practical guide to photographing and recording storm damage to your home, and what documentation is actually useful later.
articles.excerpt: Good documentation is dated, specific, and taken from the ground.

body.text: Documentation is the cheapest thing you can do after a storm and the thing people most often skip. It costs nothing, takes twenty minutes, and is far more useful now than it will be in three months.
Do it the same day if you safely can
Photos taken while debris is still in the yard and water is still on the floor carry a timestamp that connects them to a specific weather event. Photos taken later do not.
What to photograph

items: Wide shots of each elevation of the house, so location context is clear
Every dented gutter, downspout, vent housing, and window screen
AC condenser fins — flattened fins are strong hail evidence
Debris in the yard, including shingle fragments and downed limbs
Fence damage, downed sections, and damaged outbuildings
Every interior stain, drip, and damaged item, with a wide shot and a close-up of each
Standing water, saturated carpet, and damaged flooring

body.text: Include something for scale

A coin, a tape measure, or your hand next to a hailstone or a dent makes the photograph far more informative. If hail is still on the ground, photograph it against something with a known size before it melts.
Write down the basics

items: Date and approximate time the storm hit
Roughly how large the hail was and how long it fell
When you first noticed each piece of damage
Any emergency work performed, with receipts
Names and companies of anyone who came to the door

body.text: Stay off the roof

Ground-level and window photos are what you can safely produce yourself. Roof-level documentation is the job of an inspector with the equipment and the training — and for most damage types, drone imagery produces a better record than anything you would get standing on the shingles.
We can document visible damage and describe the roofing scope in writing for you to share with your carrier if you choose. Decisions about your claim are between you and your insurance company.

articles.title: Questions to Ask a Roofing Contractor
articles.metaTitle: Questions to Ask a Roofer | Timber Roofing
articles.description: The questions that separate a contractor worth hiring from one worth avoiding, especially in the weeks after a North Texas hail storm.
articles.excerpt: The right questions are short, and the answers tell you almost everything.

body.text: After a hail event, a lot of people will offer to put a roof on your house. Some of them will be gone by next spring. These questions sort that out quickly, and any honest contractor will answer them without hesitation.
About the company

items: Where are you based, and how long have you worked in this area?
Are you insured, and can you provide proof of coverage?
Who will actually be on my roof — your crew or a subcontractor?
If I have a problem in two years, who do I call, and will that number still work?

body.text: About the inspection

items: Will you show me photographs of what you found?
Which slopes have damage, and which do not?
Is this a repair or a replacement, and what makes you say so?
What is the condition of my flashing, penetrations, and ventilation?

body.text: About the work

items: Is the estimate itemized, and what exactly does it include?
Are you tearing off or going over the existing roof?
Are you replacing the flashing and pipe boots, or reusing them?
What happens if you find damaged decking?
How do you protect landscaping, windows, and the driveway?
Who cleans up, and does that include a magnet sweep?

body.text: Answers that should concern you
Any offer to cover, waive, or absorb your deductible. Any promise about what your insurance company will approve. Any pressure to sign on the doorstep. Any refusal to put the scope in writing.

Also worth noticing: a contractor who never gets on the roof, who cannot show you a photograph of the damage they are describing, or who moves to a replacement number before explaining what they found.
One more question

Ask what they would do if it were their own house. It is a simple question, and the way someone answers it — whether they reason through your specific roof or repeat a pitch — tells you most of what you need to know.
